# The Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

I've been thinking about how we've optimized the confusion out of life. GPS, predictive text, algorithm-curated feeds—we've built a world that anticipates our needs before we fully know them ourselves. It's efficient. It's also a little bit sad.

There's something irreplaceable about being genuinely lost. Not dangerously lost, but that delicious uncertainty of turning down an unfamiliar street and discovering a café you'll love, or a mural that stops you cold, or a person who becomes a friend because you both took the wrong train.

I'm not romanticizing inefficiency for its own sake. But I notice that the best stories in my life tend to start with "I had no idea where I was going." The worst ones often come from following the most logical path.

Maybe this is about control—how we've confused knowing where we're headed with actually *going* somewhere meaningful. A GPS gets you to your destination, but it doesn't teach you the route. It doesn't let you discover you're braver than you thought, or that you're terrible at reading maps, or that you like wandering.

I'm not suggesting we abandon our phones and navigation apps. But I am suggesting we get lost more deliberately. Leave early for an appointment so there's time to take a wrong turn. Skip the search results and just explore. Ask for directions from actual humans.

The world is still full of unmapped corners, still generous with surprises—but only for those willing to be a little lost.
